title: Excessively high memory usage when using client-side zstd compression in confighttp
body: I rolled out zstd compression for OTLP traffic between an agent and gateway in Kubernetes and saw the client-side otlphttp exporter use more than ten times as much memory as gzip on Collector 0.82.0. My exporter uses zstd with batch sizes of 1000/2000 and a one-second timeout on EKS. I reproduced it with a synthetic workload producing 10,000 log lines per second: gzip used 79 MiB while zstd used 469 MiB. My profiles and benchmarks suggest that zstd allocates substantial memory for each encoder and that the encoder sync.Pool is often cold because requests are not frequent enough. A test branch using a different pooling mechanism brought memory usage back to a reasonable level.

symptoms_visible: With the same 10,000-log-lines-per-second workload, kubectl top reports 79 MiB for gzip and 469 MiB for zstd.
The otlphttp exporter using zstd consumes more than ten times the memory I see with gzip.
My alternative-pooling test branch brings the observed memory usage back to a reasonable level.
N0.label: N0 client-side zstd memory increase reproduced

symptoms_visible: On Collector 0.94.0 after at least an hour, my gzip deployment uses 74 MiB and my zstd deployment uses 106 MiB.
N1.label: N1 newer-version cluster comparison collected

symptoms_visible: On Collector 0.92.0 I measure 84 MiB with gzip and 250 MiB with zstd.
On Collector 0.94.0 I measure 73 MiB with gzip and 118 MiB with zstd; the difference is smaller than before but remains visible.
N2.label: N2 version comparison shows remaining zstd overhead

symptoms_visible: The draft benchmark compares zstd memory allocation with concurrency enabled and disabled.
N3.label: N3 concurrency allocation benchmark prepared

symptoms_visible: I marked the client-side issue resolved in #9749, but I did not post a new client-side cluster memory measurement from a build containing the merged change.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix merged without post-merge client measurement

question_patterns: Can you compare gzip and zstd memory usage on a newer Collector version under a sustained workload?
Does the same memory gap occur on Collector 0.94.0?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I deployed Collector 0.94.0 with at least 50 nginx pods producing a log every second and let it run for at least an hour. kubectl top showed 74 MiB for gzip and 106 MiB for zstd.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: On 0.94.0, gzip and zstd remain more than tenfold apart under the same sustained workload.
On 0.94.0 I see 76 MiB for gzip and 108 MiB for zstd after an hour.

edges.comment: From c3, describing rnishtala-sumo's separate Kubernetes deployment. The affected operator is folded into the simulated user side; these measurements are not attributed to the opening reporter's cluster.

question_patterns: What memory readings do you get when repeating the comparison on Collector 0.92.0?
Can you provide the gzip and zstd readings from the older-version deployment?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With Collector 0.92.0, kubectl top showed 84 MiB for gzip and 250 MiB for zstd.

question_patterns: What readings do you get from another run on Collector 0.94.0?
Can you repeat the same comparison on the newer version?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With Collector 0.94.0, another run showed 73 MiB for gzip and 118 MiB for zstd.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: On 0.94.0, gzip and zstd have essentially identical memory use across repeated runs.
The repeated 0.94.0 run differs by a few MiB but still leaves zstd clearly above gzip.

edges.comment: From c4, again describing rnishtala-sumo's deployment and folded into the user side. The same comment volunteered that 0.94.0 uses compress v1.17.5 and linked prior sync.Pool/concurrency leak research; those facts enter N2 as volunteered information rather than conclusions hidden in the measurement answers.

question_patterns: Can you add an allocation benchmark that compares the proposed zstd configurations?
Do we have a benchmark that makes the memory-allocation difference visible?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I created draft PR #9749 with a benchmark comparing zstd memory allocation with concurrency enabled and disabled.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The benchmark shows no meaningful allocation difference between the two configurations.
The allocation difference is visible but varies between benchmark runs because the sync.Pool behavior is timing-sensitive.

edges.comment: From c5-c8: atoulme requested a benchmark, rnishtala-sumo agreed to compare the configurations and created draft PR #9749. The answer reports only the benchmark artifact and comparison performed; the causal interpretation remains engineer-side.

solution.intent: Reduce client-side zstd encoder memory by disabling its default parallel concurrency, so repeatedly created or cold-pooled encoders do not each retain the much larger concurrent working set.
solution.concrete_example: Configure the confighttp client-side zstd encoder to run with concurrency disabled, as implemented and benchmarked in #9749, rather than relying on the default concurrent encoder behavior inside a timing-sensitive sync.Pool.
solution.inference_hint: The benchmark artifact, cluster readings and reporter's pooling experiment are user-side evidence. Concluding that default zstd encoder concurrency multiplies the per-encoder working set when sync.Pool reuse is unreliable—and therefore selecting single-threaded client encoding—is the final engineering inference embodied by #9749.

edges.comment: Resolution from c9: the opening reporter stated that the original client-side issue was resolved in #9749. No affected user posted a post-merge client-side memory retest, so the terminal remains unverified from the user's perspective. Comments c10-c14 concern a later server-side receiver/crash problem on a different deployment and are deliberately excluded from this causal chain; c11 asks that it be filed separately.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted client-side cause: default zstd encoder concurrency creates a large per-encoder memory cost that is amplified when timing-sensitive sync.Pool reuse is ineffective and encoders are repeatedly created.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the gzip-versus-zstd Kubernetes readings, the cold-pool hypothesis, the successful alternative-pooling experiment, and the benchmark comparing concurrency configurations.

The fix must disable parallel concurrency for the client-side zstd encoder rather than treating the compress-library upgrade alone as sufficient; newer-library runs improved the numbers but still left zstd above gzip.
Must not conflate the later server-side HTTP receiver crash or panic reports with this original client-side exporter memory chain.
Must ask an affected user to verify memory consumption on a build containing the fix and must not claim that post-merge client-side verification occurred in this thread.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced Go and OpenTelemetry contributor who can reproduce production behavior in Kubernetes, collect memory profiles, write synthetic benchmarks, inspect sync.Pool behavior, and prototype alternative pooling implementations.
persona_hint.communication_style: Technical, evidence-driven, and cautious about causal claims; provides concrete resource readings and code links, distinguishes an effective experiment from a fully understood explanation, and follows up when time permits.
